# Briefly | AI knowledge base for financial advisors, inside Claude
Source: https://www.brieflywealth.com/

**AI knowledge base for RIAs and advisor teams**

# Ask your firm's files anything.

Briefly turns the statements, emails, and meeting notes your firm already has into one knowledge base. Ask inside Claude or in the Briefly web app, and every answer comes back cited. Fix something once, and it holds for the whole team from then on.

Run the connector and client files never reach our servers. Or have us set up the web app, connected to your Salesforce and Outlook.

Correct a phrase once, and every brief your firm gets from then on says it your way.

## Ten years of files, one working memory.

Briefly is an AI knowledge base for financial advisors that runs inside Claude. The answers your firm needs are already sitting in folders, inboxes, and old plans. Briefly files each document into the right client's knowledge base as it arrives, and every fact keeps a link back to the page it came from. The more you add, the better every answer gets.

A Henderson, David & Priya client file shows what that looks like once documents are filed. 84 documents, updated today. The 401(k) rollover completed at $412,000, cited to the Q2 statement. An open K-1 question with the CPA, cited to a June 12 email. A goal to fund the lake house by 2028, cited to a June 14 transcript. An umbrella policy renewing in September, cited to the renewal notice.

## In Claude, or in a web app we set up for you.

Same knowledge base, same citations. What changes is who does the setup and where your team asks.

### The Claude connector

Runs inside the Claude your team already uses. Client files never reach our servers. Every answer cites its source document. Learns your firm's corrections as standing rules. Ask across your whole book, not one chat. Sign up today, no call needed. Checkout takes a card but charges nothing for 30 days, and you can cancel from the billing portal any time.

### The web app

We build the client file for you. Connects your Salesforce and Outlook. Approved next steps route back into Salesforce. Sign in from a browser, nothing for IT to install.

Run both and a seat moves between them without rebuilding anything, since it is one client file either way. You can sign up for the connector without talking to anyone. Pick your seats, check out, and download the connector. The first charge lands on day 31, and you can cancel any time before that. Payments run on Stripe, so Briefly never sees your card.

## You choose where your files live, and they stay yours either way.

Most AI tools for advisors upload your client data to their servers and promise to protect it. Briefly gives you two ways to run it, and both put the choice in your hands.

### The connector: files stay on your machines.

Briefly builds the knowledge base in your firm's own folders and Claude reads it right there, on your plan. Only your sign-in, a seat check, de-identified preference rules, and a short usage record for each tool call ever reach Briefly.

### The web app: files live with us, locked down.

We build the client file for you in an environment we secure and control. Your team signs in from a browser, and your firm decides who gets a seat.

Either way, Briefly doesn't use client data to train AI models, and a seat can move between the two without rebuilding anything.

## One day with the file open.

Briefly isn't a new place to work. Your team keeps asking questions where they already are, and the firm's own records do the answering.

**8:55 am, in Claude, before the review.** The advisor asks, "Give me the Patel file before the 9:00." Briefly returns a prepared brief, three open items, one sentiment shift since April, and the rollover question still waiting on their HR paperwork, cited to six sources.

**11:40 am, in the web app, a client calls.** Operations asks, "Did we ever get the updated beneficiary form from the Kims?" Briefly answers yes, signed copy filed in March, primary changed to their daughter, cited to the beneficiary form filed March 19, 2026.

**4:15 pm, in Claude, across the book.** The advisor asks, "Which households have mentioned selling a business?" Briefly finds four households, each with the conversation it came from, cited to four sources across four files. Two mentioned a timeline inside three years.

## Correct it once. The whole firm inherits it.

When an advisor fixes a name, a preference, or a way of phrasing things, Briefly keeps the fix as a standing rule. Next quarter's brief already follows it, for everyone. An advisor at one firm fixed a single phrase, "we call it a planning conversation, never a sales meeting." Every brief that firm has received since says it their way.

## What Ask Briefly answers.

The web app's Ask Briefly surface answers cross-client and single-household questions with numbered sources and a one-click receipt back to the original document. Five examples the homepage cycles through, drawn from the page's own crawlable question set.

Q: What changed for the Hendersons since our March review?

Two things. The 401(k) rollover completed at $412,000, and their CPA flagged an open K-1 question in June. Both are filed and linked, cited to the Henderson Q2 statement (filed 6/30/2026) and a CPA email from M. Hill (filed 6/12/2026).

Q: Which clients hold a concentrated position above 20%?

Three households. Rivera at 31% in employer stock, Okafor at 24%, and Lindqvist at 22%, each read from the latest statement on file, cited to their Q2 and Q1 statements.

Q: Who mentioned wanting to retire in the next three years?

Four clients, each tied to the conversation where they said it. Two of them also asked about pension timing, noted in their files and cited to meeting transcripts for the Doyle and Chen households, plus two more conversations.

Q: What's still open from last week's client meetings?

Five follow-ups across four households, from a missing insurance rider to the Whitfield trust question, each naming the meeting it came from, cited to the Whitfield transcript (filed 7/24/2026) and four more items.

Q: Anything I should know before the Alvarez call at 2:00?

Their daughter's tuition starts this fall, the 529 is short of the plan, and Maria sounded frustrated about paperwork last visit. The prepared brief covers all three, cited to a 529 plan review (filed 6/3/2026), call notes (filed 7/17/2026), and the Alvarez pre-call brief.

## What advisors ask us first.

Q: Is my client data safe?

With the connector, client files stay on your computer and our servers never store them. What does reach us stays at the account level, your sign-in, a seat check, de-identified preference rules, and a short usage record for each tool call. On the AI side, Claude reads the file under your firm's own Claude plan, and on business plans Anthropic's commercial terms bar training on customer content. We don't train AI models on client data either. Firms that choose the hosted version keep their files in an environment we secure and control, and the firm decides who signs in.

Q: Can I put client data into ChatGPT or Claude?

Pasting client details into a personal AI chat window sends them to the vendor's servers under consumer terms your firm never reviewed. The SEC's amended Reg S-P rule requires firms to oversee the service providers that handle customer information, which is why compliance teams are asking about AI chat tools. With the Briefly connector, client files stay in your firm's own folders and Claude reads them under the Claude plan your firm chose and can review like any other vendor.

Q: Why not just use Claude or ChatGPT on their own?

AI models change every few months, and what a chat window learned about your firm doesn't carry over. Briefly organizes your firm's knowledge into plain files you own, so the context you build keeps working as models improve or get swapped out. Answers draw on your whole book, corrections hold, and every claim carries a citation you can open.

Q: Which one should I pick?

If your team already works in Claude, start with the connector. It reads folders on your own machines and answers where you already work. If you want the file built for you, take the web app. We connect Salesforce and Outlook and your team signs in from a browser. A seat can move between them without rebuilding anything.

Q: How long does setup take?

The connector installs like any Claude connector and reads the folders you point it at, so most teams are asking questions the same day. The hosted version takes longer because we connect Salesforce and Outlook and build the client file for you.

Q: What happens if I leave?

With the connector there is nothing to migrate, because the files were always in your own folders. Removing it just stops Claude from reading them. On the hosted version, your firm has ninety days after leaving to export its files in a standard format, and after that window we delete them.

See it answer on your firm's own records. Twenty minutes, with the advisor in the room. No call needed for the connector, start now and you're asking questions today. Not ready? Get the Morning Brief, a daily market email for advisors.

# AI Knowledge Base for Financial Advisors | Briefly

**Knowledge Base**

# An AI knowledge base for financial advisors that runs inside Claude.

By Connor Florczyk. Updated August 5, 2026.

Client documents, email, and meeting notes already sit inside your firm. Briefly turns them into one knowledge base that Claude can read across every account in your book. Ask which clients hold a concentrated position over $500K and get an answer with a name, a number, and the statement it came from, the same way you'd get an answer about one household.

A sample cross-client query, "Which clients hold a concentrated position over $500K?" Rivera, $684,300 in employer stock (31%), Q2 statement. Okafor, $558,900 in a single legacy position (24%), Q2 statement. Lindqvist, $511,000 in concentrated equity (22%), Q1 statement.

Wealth firms already have plenty of data. Client facts live across CRM records, emails, meeting notes, custodial statements, financial plans, and spreadsheets, plus whatever an advisor happens to remember, and none of those systems share a model of the relationship.

A knowledge base gives the firm that model. It connects people, households, entities, accounts, goals, concerns, events, tasks, and source citations, so every workflow starts from the same understanding of the client. Ask a question about one household or about every household in the book, and the answer comes from the same place.

Sources, emails, notes, meetings, PDFs, CRM records, portfolio data, and planning documents, resolve into the knowledge base, resolved people, households, entities, relationships, tasks, goals, and evidence, which shows up wherever the advisor is working, inside Claude through the connector, or in the Briefly web app if Briefly sets it up.

## Ask across your whole book, not one client file.

Most tools answer a question about whatever client file happens to be open. Briefly checks every household in your book for the same question, then answers it the way it would answer about one client, with a name, a number, and the document behind it.

Asked once, "Which clients hold a concentrated position above $500K?", Briefly checks every household in the book, not just the one open on screen, and answers. Rivera holds $684,300 in employer stock, 31% of the account. Okafor holds $558,900 in a single legacy position, 24%. Lindqvist holds $511,000 in concentrated equity, 22%. Each figure links back to the document it came from, Rivera's Q2 statement filed July 8, Okafor's Q2 statement filed July 2, Lindqvist's Q1 statement filed April 14.

The same pattern holds for any cross-client question, whether it's about concentrated positions, upcoming distributions, or clients who mentioned selling a business. This works because every document lands in a household's own record first, then gets checked across the whole book whenever a question calls for it. Filing an email into the Rivera file also becomes one of the records checked the next time someone asks about concentrated positions or anything else that spans the book, something a CRM field or a folder of PDFs can't do on its own.

## Why this matters in wealth management.

Households are becoming more complex as wealth transfers across generations.

Advisors are responsible for more relationships without proportional support staff.

What advisors know about a client often stays in individual memory instead of firm infrastructure.

Generic AI summaries are risky unless they are traceable to source material.

Briefly is built to answer inside that reality without asking a firm to change how it works. It runs inside Claude, where many advisor teams are already working, and reads the files that are already there. If a firm runs the connector, those files stay on the advisor's own computer, and the only things that reach Briefly's servers are your sign-in, a seat check, de-identified preference rules, and a short usage record for each tool call, never the client file itself. That's true whether the question comes up during meeting prep the morning of, or mid-call about a household nobody on the call remembers well.

## Why CRMs are not enough.

CRMs are important systems of record, but they are not built to reconstruct a relationship across every source. The details that matter most often live in a note, a forwarded email, a PDF, a meeting transcript, a planning document, or the memory of a senior advisor.

Search helps when you already know what to look for. A knowledge base helps when you need the system to surface what matters before you ask.

A CRM also only knows what someone typed into it. It doesn't read the email you forwarded, the PDF you saved to a folder, or the transcript from last week's call, not unless someone copies the details in by hand. Briefly reads those files directly, so the knowledge base grows every time a document gets filed, not every time someone remembers to update a record.

Neither one learns from being corrected. If an advisor tells a CRM once that a client goes by a nickname, or that the firm calls it a planning conversation and never a sales meeting, someone has to remember to make the same fix again the next time it comes up. Briefly keeps a correction like that as a standing rule instead. One firm did exactly this with a single phrase, telling Briefly to say planning conversation instead of sales meeting, and every brief that firm has received since has followed it, for every advisor on the team.

"Your brain does not have enough RAM for this job."

## What a knowledge base should include.

Family and household relationships, including heirs and decision makers.

Professional network, including CPAs, attorneys, trustees, and centers of influence.

Planning themes such as liquidity, philanthropy, estate complexity, concentrated positions, and tax deadlines.

Open loops, follow-ups, unresolved concerns, and promises made in prior meetings.

Source citations so advisors can verify before using anything with a client.

None of this shows up on its own. A knowledge base only holds what gets filed into it, so the categories above are really a checklist for what to point Briefly at first, statements, planning documents, and the emails and notes an advisor already has sitting in a folder.

## A meeting brief is one thing the knowledge base can do.

A meeting brief is useful because it gives the advisor an edge before the conversation starts, but the brief draws on the same knowledge base behind the whole-book questions above it. Open tasks, portfolio changes, client sentiment, life events, and the professional network around a client all come from files that were filed for other reasons first. The brief just pulls the relevant pieces together and cites where each one came from. See an actual brief, with names and firms changed, on the sample deliverables page.

Each meeting adds more source-backed memory to the knowledge base, and meeting prep gets faster with every cycle because there's less new material to review each time. The client file gets richer, and the firm becomes less dependent on any one person's memory.

## What Briefly builds.

Briefly turns fragmented advisor files into a living knowledge base. It keeps every fact traceable to its source, keeps outputs reviewable, and gives each workflow what it needs without forcing a CRM migration.

Each new document, an email forwarded from a client, a statement uploaded after it arrives, a note typed up after a call, gets filed into the household it belongs to and read into the knowledge base right away. Nothing has to be reformatted or copied into a separate system first.

Briefly runs two ways, inside Claude with the connector or as a web app Briefly sets up. Either way it's the same knowledge base underneath, built from the same files, with the same citations on every answer. The result is one base of firm memory. It gets better every time an advisor uses it, and it keeps working long after any single meeting ends.

### Connor Florczyk

Founder of Briefly. Before Briefly, he worked as a private wealth analyst on a top-performing team at Morgan Stanley, where he saw firsthand how much advisor time gets lost hunting for a client's own files.

Your firm's memory, from your own files.

Download Briefly. Mac & Windows. Requires Claude. By downloading and installing the connector, you agree to the Connector EULA.

Using Briefly starts with a login Briefly sets up for you. Download first, then book a demo so Briefly sets up your firm's sign-in. From there your whole team shares how your firm likes its briefs written.

Not sure what you're about to open? This page installs the Briefly connector, which adds Briefly to Claude Desktop. One download, pick a folder on your computer, sign in, and you're set up. Client files stay in that folder. Briefly's servers only see your sign-in, a seat check, de-identified preference rules, and a short usage record for each tool call, never a client file. If your firm would rather work from a browser with no install, Briefly also has a web app with its own sign-in.

## Five minutes, start to finish.

Five steps, use the dots to jump ahead.

### Step 1: Get Claude

Free from claude.ai. Skip this step if you already have it. The walkthrough shows the Claude download page, the download completing, and the installer dragging Claude into Applications.

### Step 2: Download Briefly

One click on brieflywealth.com/download, then open it from your browser's downloads. Shown in Chrome, in Safari downloads live under the arrow next to the address bar. Open the downloaded briefly_wealth.mcpb file to launch Claude Desktop, then click Install."

### Step 3: Claude installs it

Click Install, then Save. Nothing to type. The settings screen is optional, save and move on. The red Anthropic notice is standard for extensions installed outside its directory. The walkthrough shows the Briefly extension detail page inside Claude Desktop. Description, "A source-backed knowledge base for financial advisors. Reads the firm's files and answers with citations. The Claude work runs on the firm's own plan." A banner warns that installing grants the extension access to everything on the computer. 37 tools are listed, including briefly_ask, briefly_get_recent_activity, briefly_prepare_meeting_brief, briefly_resolve_citation, briefly_get_advisor_learning_profile, briefly_ingest_source, briefly_update_entity, and briefly_capture. A native "Do you want to install Briefly?" confirmation dialog appears, then a Configure screen with two optional fields, "Your firm's folder" and "Inbox folder." Saving raises a toast, "Briefly added to Claude."

### Step 4: Sign in once

Your login is the whole setup. Use the login set up for your firm, and Briefly knows you and your firm. The walkthrough shows a Claude conversation, "What do we have on file for the Johnsons?", triggering a sign-in page at auth.brieflywealth.com.

### Step 5: File, then brief

Save statements into the intake folder, then ask, "File everything in my intake folder." Then, "Prepare a meeting brief." The walkthrough shows a Finder window with a Briefly folder (wiki, operating, originals, intake, sources) receiving two filed PDF statements, then a Claude conversation where Briefly confirms it filed both for the Johnson family, with originals routed to originals/johnson-family/, a Schwab balance of $1,284,306.22 and a Vanguard IRA balance of $612,940.18, each cited, followed by a prepared meeting brief giving a household net worth of $1,897,246.40 and a largest position of AAPL at 11.2% of the brokerage account, sourced to the Schwab and Vanguard statements.

With the Briefly connector, your original files stay on your machine. Briefly saves them in your folder, builds every brief locally, and never uploads your files. The finished brief is written by your own Claude, so its content follows your Claude plan and privacy settings. The web app works differently, since its files live in Briefly's hosted environment.

Works in Claude Desktop on macOS and Windows.

## Questions before you install.

Q: Do I need Claude to use Briefly?

Yes. Briefly is a connector you add to Claude Desktop. You need the free Claude Desktop app installed first, then Briefly plugs into it. If you already use Claude for chat or writing, it's the same app, and Briefly reads your client files from inside it.

Q: Where do my client files live?

With the Briefly connector, client files live on your computer, in a folder you pick during setup. Briefly reads and writes files there directly, and nothing gets uploaded to a Briefly database or cloud storage account. The browser web app works differently. Its files live in Briefly's hosted environment instead.

Q: Is this a web app?

Briefly comes in two forms, and this page installs the Claude connector, where your team runs Briefly inside Claude reading folders on your own machines. With the web app, Briefly connects your Salesforce and Outlook and builds the client file for you, so there's nothing for your IT to install.

Q: What does Briefly's server see?

With the Claude connector, our server sees your sign-in, a seat check, de-identified preference rules your firm builds over time, never tied to a client name, and a short usage record for each tool call. Client files never reach our servers. The web app differs, since its files live on our side instead.

Q: Does Briefly work on Windows and Mac?

Yes, both. The same download and the same install steps work on macOS and Windows. Claude Desktop also has a Linux beta on Ubuntu and Debian, though we haven't certified Briefly there yet.

Q: How long does setup take?

About five minutes if you already have Claude Desktop installed. Download Briefly, open the file, click Install in Claude, sign in, and point it at a folder on your computer. That's the whole process, a handful of clicks with no IT ticket and no server setup required.

Ready when you are. Download Briefly.

# Security | Briefly
Source: https://www.brieflywealth.com/security
---

**Security**

# With the Briefly connector, client files stay on the advisor's computer.

Briefly is an AI knowledge base for financial advisors. It runs two ways, a connector inside Claude Desktop and a hosted web app you sign into through your browser. This page lays out where your client files live on each surface, what reaches our servers, and what changes under the new SEC rules for AI vendors.

Briefly's flagship product is a connector you add to Claude Desktop. One download, pick a folder on your computer, sign in, and you're set up. From there, your client files stay in that folder, not on a server somewhere. When you ask Briefly a question, it reads those files on your machine, writes the answer, and saves the draft back to the same folder. The only things that reach our servers are your sign-in, a seat check, de-identified preference rules that never carry a client's name, and a short usage record for each tool call, which carries no client file content.

Some firms run Briefly a second way, through the web app you sign into instead of installing the connector. It's priced and sold separately from the connector. For firms on the web app, client files live in Briefly's hosted environment on AWS, protected by per-firm access controls, and sign-in runs through the same account layer either way.

## Where your client files live on the connector

For firms running the connector, there's no upload step in Briefly. You point it at a folder once, during setup, and everything after that happens on your own machine.

### You choose the folder

During setup, you pick where on your computer Briefly reads and writes. It's a folder your firm already uses, not a location Briefly assigns.

### Nothing to upload

Briefly runs inside Claude Desktop and works with files already on your machine. There's no button or portal that sends a client file anywhere.

### No client-file database for connector firms

Briefly doesn't operate a database of client files for firms on the connector. If someone got into Briefly's servers, there's no trove of those firms' client documents there for them to find.

## What reaches Briefly's server, when you run the connector

Four things reach our servers when you run the connector, and none of them is a client file. The web app works differently, covered below.

### Sign-in

Briefly checks who you are through Amazon Cognito, the identity system a large share of the software industry runs on. This confirms it's you, not anything about a client.

### Seat and entitlement checks

Briefly checks that your firm's account is active and your seat is licensed before it does any work. It's a subscription check, the kind any paid software runs.

### De-identified preference rules

Briefly learns patterns in how your firm likes its work done. Those patterns are tokenized before they leave your computer, so no client name or account number is attached to them.

### A usage record for each tool call

Each time you run a Briefly tool, Briefly logs a short record of that call, the tool, the outcome, and a timestamp, tied to your seat and firm. It carries no content from your client files.

On the connector, client files never reach Briefly's servers. Only your sign-in, a seat check, de-identified preference rules, and a short usage record for each tool call reach Briefly's server, and none of it carries anything about a specific client. Firms on the web app work under a different model, laid out below.

## What Claude sees, and what Anthropic does with it

Briefly runs inside Claude, so a careful vendor review should ask about Anthropic too. Here is the full path, with nothing left out.

When an advisor asks a question, Claude reads the parts of the client file it needs to answer, straight from the folder on the advisor's computer. Anthropic processes that content to generate the answer, under your firm's own Claude agreement. Briefly never stores it, and it never touches Briefly's servers.

This is why the Claude plan matters. On Claude for Work, Claude Enterprise, and the API, Anthropic's commercial terms prohibit training models on customer content. That is a contract term, and it comes with a data processing agreement your vendor-oversight file can hold. Deleted conversations purge from Anthropic's systems within 30 days. The exception is content flagged by Anthropic's safety systems, which it can hold for up to two years. Briefly recommends firms run Briefly on a business Claude plan.

Personal Claude plans work differently, and the difference is worth writing down. Conversations on a Free, Pro, or Max account train Anthropic's models unless training is turned off in privacy settings, and content used for training is kept for up to five years. Anthropic's July 2026 policy update also allows conversations flagged by its safety systems to be used for model improvement even after a user opts out, with flagged content held for up to two years. An advisor can run Briefly this way, and a compliance officer will reasonably prefer the business plan's written terms.

One more fact a thorough vendor review will surface. Since June 2026, even Anthropic's zero-retention API arrangements carry a 30-day retention window on its newest models for safety monitoring. No tool built on a frontier model can honestly promise that nothing is ever retained, so the questions worth asking a vendor are where files are stored, whose agreement governs the processing, and what the vendor itself holds.

The short version for a vendor file. Client files are stored only in your folder. Processing happens under your firm's own Claude agreement, and on a business plan Anthropic may not train on your content by contract. Briefly's servers only ever see your sign-in, a seat check, de-identified preference rules, and a short usage record for each tool call.

## Three ways advisor AI tools handle your data

Every AI tool that touches client files falls into one of three custody models, and Briefly's two surfaces land in two different ones.

**Cloud AI tools.** Files get uploaded to the vendor's servers. From there, the vendor's privacy policy decides what happens next, including how long files sit there and who can review them. You're trusting a policy, not an architecture.

**Briefly web app.** Your firm signs in through a browser, and files live in Briefly's hosted environment on AWS, with access controls scoped to your firm. It's server-side custody, the same category as a hosted private AI tool, except Briefly is the one running it.

**Briefly connector.** Client files stay in a folder on the advisor's own computer. There's no upload and no server-side client-file store, so there's nothing of yours on our servers for a breach to reach.

## What this means under Reg S-P

SEC privacy and safeguards rules, Reg S-P among them, put the duty on advisory firms to know how their vendors handle customer information, and firms are treating AI tools as part of that vendor review. That oversight duty sits with your firm, not just with Briefly.

Both the SEC and FINRA have said publicly that they are watching how firms use and supervise AI. The practical effect is that the vendor relationship gets reviewed, not only the advisor's own desk.

No agency certifies an AI tool as SEC-approved. That label doesn't exist. What a firm can document is how a specific tool actually handles client data, which is what the rest of this page lays out.

## How we secure the account layer

For connector firms, client files aren't on our servers, so what Briefly secures there is narrower, the sign-in and entitlement system that confirms who you are and what your firm has access to. Web-app firms have files in our hosted environment too, secured the way the custody section above describes.

### Sign-in

Access runs through Amazon Cognito, the identity system described above, on both surfaces. Every session ties back to your individual login and your firm's account, not a shared password.

### No client-file database to isolate on the connector

For connector firms, there's no per-firm client-file database on our servers to isolate, because those files never reach our servers in the first place. For web-app firms, per-firm access controls scope each firm to its own data. Sign-in and preference records are isolated at the application level for every firm.

### Encrypted transport and vendor review

Sign-in and entitlement traffic between your computer and our servers runs over encrypted connections. Briefly reviews the vendors behind that layer, including AWS and Cognito, the way it would want a vendor it depends on reviewed.

### SOC 2 aligned controls

Briefly's security program is built around the SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria, applied to the systems Briefly actually runs, sign-in and entitlement. Formal certification is on the roadmap, not yet in audit.

## Compliance officer FAQ

Q: Where exactly do client files live?

It depends on which surface your firm runs. On the connector, files stay in a folder on the advisor's own computer that Briefly reads from and writes back to. On the web app, files live in Briefly's hosted environment on AWS, with access scoped to your firm's account.

Q: Does Anthropic see client files when Briefly runs inside Claude?

When an advisor asks a question, Claude reads what it needs from the client file, and Anthropic processes that content under your firm's own Claude plan. On business plans, Anthropic's commercial terms prohibit training on customer content, and deleted conversations purge within 30 days, except content flagged by Anthropic's safety systems. Briefly never stores what Claude reads.

Q: What does Briefly's server actually receive?

It depends on the surface. From the connector, Briefly's server receives your sign-in through Amazon Cognito, a seat-active check, de-identified preference rules, and a short usage record for each tool call, which carries no client file content. From the web app, your firm's files also reach our hosted environment, because that's how the product runs on that surface.

Q: Does Briefly train AI models on client data?

No, on either surface. Client data is used to run the product for your firm, not to train general-purpose AI models, and any pattern-level learning Briefly does runs through a de-identified, tokenized layer with no client name or account number attached.

Q: Is Briefly a web app my staff logs into?

Both exist. The connector runs inside Claude Desktop and works with files already on the advisor's computer, without an upload step, just a one-time sign-in. The web app is a separate, browser-based product your staff can sign into instead, priced separately, with files hosted in Briefly's own environment rather than on your machine.

Q: What happens if Briefly's servers are breached?

For connector firms, a breach exposes sign-in records, seat-check records, de-identified preference rules, and usage records, not client files, since those never reach our servers. For web-app firms, Briefly's hosted environment does hold firm data, protected by encryption and per-firm access controls, so the exposure model is different for that surface.

Q: How does this change our Reg S-P vendor due diligence?

Firms generally review Briefly as a service provider under Reg S-P, the same as any vendor. For connector firms, client files never reach our servers, so what our side holds for that review is sign-in, seat entitlement, the preference layer, and usage records, with no client-data store. The model call runs under your firm's own Claude plan, laid out earlier on this page. For web-app firms, the review also takes in Briefly's AWS hosting and per-firm access controls, the way any hosted vendor gets reviewed.

Q: Is Briefly SEC-approved or certified compliant?

No certification like that exists, and no agency approves an AI tool as compliant. What Briefly can show you is exactly how its architecture, on either the connector or the web app, handles client data, which is the purpose of this page.

This page describes Briefly's architecture and general regulatory background for information only. It is not legal or compliance advice. Review any AI tool with your own counsel or compliance officer.

Need a security review? Contact contact@brieflywealth.com for architecture, vendor, and data-processing questions, including security and vulnerability reports.

# ChatGPT and Claude Compliance for Financial Advisors | Briefly
Source: https://www.brieflywealth.com/ai-compliance-for-financial-advisors
---

**Compliance**

# Can financial advisors put client data in ChatGPT?

By Connor Florczyk. Published July 23, 2026. Last verified August 5, 2026.

A straight answer for advisors and compliance officers weighing ChatGPT, Claude, and the rules that actually govern where client data can go.

The direct answer is yes, you can type a client's name, account number, or portfolio detail into ChatGPT's chat window, and the harder question is whether your compliance program has ever looked at where that text goes. It travels to a vendor's servers under that vendor's own policy, not your firm's, and the SEC's updated privacy rules require firms to oversee the service providers that handle customer information. Advisors can still use ChatGPT and Claude for real work. The rest of this page covers what the rules say and the setup that gets advisors the benefit of these tools while keeping their compliance program in the loop. None of it is legal advice, and your compliance officer or counsel gets the final word on your firm's own obligations.

Advisors are asking this question more because ChatGPT and Claude have gotten good enough to be genuinely useful for drafting, summarizing, and research, in the same twelve months the amended Reg S-P safeguards rule reached every RIA and FINRA published its first dedicated guidance on generative AI. The tools got more tempting and the rules got more specific at the same time, so the honest answer needs both halves.

## Can you put client data in ChatGPT?

Physically, yes. Nothing in ChatGPT's interface stops you from pasting a client's name, account number, holdings, or a paraphrased summary of their situation into the chat box, and the model will answer. The real question for an advisor is what happens to that information after you hit enter, not whether typing it in is technically possible.

That text is sent to OpenAI's servers to generate a response, and from there, what happens depends on your plan and your settings rather than anything your firm controls. A Free or Plus account may use the conversation to train future models unless training is turned off in Data Controls settings. ChatGPT Team, Enterprise, and business API access don't train on your data by default. Either way, the information has left your firm's systems and landed on infrastructure your compliance program has probably never reviewed.

Some firms have gone further and licensed ChatGPT Enterprise for the whole office, treating that as the fix. It solves the training question and adds admin-level retention controls, but it doesn't automatically solve the other two problems on this page. The firm still needs to review OpenAI as a vendor under Reg S-P, and it still needs a way to capture AI-assisted client communications in its own archiving system.

This shows up in ordinary moments, not just theoretical ones. An advisor answering a quick client question from their phone, using the free ChatGPT app because it's already installed, creates the same exposure as an advisor pasting a full case file into the desktop version.

Some advisors try to soften this by stripping names and account numbers before pasting, asking about "a client with a $2 million portfolio and two grown children" instead of naming anyone. That reduces the privacy exposure meaningfully and works fine for a hypothetical research question with no real client attached. It doesn't solve the recordkeeping question in the next section on its own, and it only works if the advisor remembers to redact every single time.

That's the part regulators care about. Reg S-P doesn't ask whether ChatGPT is a good or bad product. It asks whether the firm knows where customer information goes and runs a real oversight process for every vendor that touches it.

## Is it safe to use ChatGPT for client emails?

Client emails carry two separate risks when they run through a consumer AI tool, and most advisors only think about one of them.

The first is privacy. An email to a client often names an account number, a balance, a beneficiary, or a specific holding. Pasting that email into ChatGPT to fix the tone or tighten the wording sends all of it to OpenAI's servers the moment you hit enter, the same category of exposure Reg S-P expects a firm to oversee as it would any other outside vendor.

The second risk gets missed more often. A client email is a business communication. FINRA member firms have to retain and supervise those communications the same way they retain any other correspondence about a client's account, and RIAs carry a parallel recordkeeping duty under the Investment Advisers Act. A conversation that happens inside a personal ChatGPT account usually isn't captured by the firm's archiving system at all. If a client complains, or an examiner asks for the correspondence file, the AI-assisted draft is often just missing.

The same exposure covers more than typed text, too. Uploading a PDF statement, a screenshot of a client's account dashboard, or a scanned form into ChatGPT to summarize it sends the entire document to the vendor's servers, not just the sentence you needed answered.

## What Reg S-P, the SEC, and FINRA actually require

Four separate pieces of the regulatory picture apply here, and the fourth explains why no vendor gets to claim it solved the other three for you.

### The amended Reg S-P safeguards rule

The SEC adopted amendments to Regulation S-P in May 2024, extending the safeguards and disposal rules that used to apply mainly to broker-dealers to registered investment advisers, investment companies, and transfer agents as well. Larger firms had to comply by December 3, 2025, and the deadline for smaller advisory firms landed June 3, 2026, which means every RIA is now inside the rule regardless of size. Covered firms need a written incident response program, a documented process for reviewing the third-party vendors that touch customer information, and a notification clock. Firms generally have to tell affected individuals about a breach as soon as practical, and within 30 days once they learn sensitive customer information was exposed. The disposal side of the same rule matters just as much. Firms have to dispose of customer information securely once it's no longer needed, and that duty doesn't disappear just because a copy sits on a vendor's server instead of the firm's own drive. An AI vendor that receives client data now falls inside that vendor review.

### The SEC's exam priorities for fiscal year 2026

The SEC's Division of Examinations released its 2026 priorities in November 2025, and artificial intelligence made the list as an area of increased focus. Examiners are checking whether a firm's actual use of AI matches what it discloses to clients and regulators, reviewing the security controls firms use to manage AI-related risk, and running sweep exams of firms most likely to have adopted AI early, including robo-advisers and algorithmic trading funds. The priorities also expect firms to have an AI policy in their compliance manual, whether that's a standalone document or a section added to an existing one.

### FINRA's 2026 regulatory oversight report

FINRA published its 2026 Annual Regulatory Oversight Report in December 2025 with a dedicated section on generative AI for the first time. The report expects member firms to assess their regulatory obligations before deploying a GenAI tool, build a governance framework around how it gets supervised, and test for hallucinations and bias rather than trust the output. The most common use FINRA observed among member firms was summarizing documents and pulling information out of large volumes of text, close to what an advisor is doing when they paste a client email into ChatGPT to redraft it.

### The AI-washing enforcement actions, and why there's no "SEC-approved AI"

In March 2024 the SEC fined two investment advisers, Delphia and Global Predictions, a combined $400,000, $225,000 from Delphia and $175,000 from Global Predictions, for overstating the role artificial intelligence played in how they managed money, the industry's first enforcement action for what regulators now call AI-washing. No AI vendor, not ChatGPT's maker, not Claude's maker, not Briefly, carries an SEC seal of approval, because that seal doesn't exist.

Put together, these four things point to the same short list of questions firms are working through with their compliance officers. Which AI tools are advisors actually using, beyond the ones the firm officially licenses? Does an AI vendor that receives client data get the same review as any other vendor? Does a written policy name the approved tools and the boundaries around them? And does a vendor's compliance-sounding language hold up against the actual rule text?

## Six questions worth putting to any AI vendor

- Where do client files or details go once the tool processes them? The disposal rule under Reg S-P still applies even when a copy sits on a vendor's server instead of your own drive.
- Whose agreement governs the processing, a business contract or a personal consumer account? A real vendor review needs a data processing agreement on file, not a terms-of-service click.
- Does the vendor train future models on your conversations, and can that be turned off? Free and Plus-tier defaults can differ from what a business plan commits to in writing.
- What does the vendor keep after you delete a conversation or opt out of training? The safeguards rule's disposal duty means your firm needs to know what a vendor holds onto, not just what it promises to delete.
- Is there a written incident-response commitment behind this vendor relationship? The amended Reg S-P rule requires a written incident response program and a notification clock, not an assumption that the vendor has one.
- Can your firm archive this tool's conversations the way it archives other client communications? FINRA's books-and-records duty covers an AI-assisted client conversation the same as any other correspondence.

The checklist above works for any AI vendor your firm is weighing. See how Briefly answers these questions on the security page, since that's the one vendor Briefly can speak to firsthand.

## What about Claude?

Claude raises a version of the same question, with one extra layer. Anthropic sells Claude across several plans, and the plan determines what happens to your conversations. The difference between the two paths is bigger than most advisors realize, and one of them is far easier for a compliance program to document.

On the business side, Anthropic's commercial terms state it plainly. Anthropic may not train models on customer content from Claude for Work, Claude Enterprise, or the API. The commitment sits in the contract itself rather than in a settings toggle, and it comes with a data processing agreement a compliance program can actually file. Deleted conversations purge from Anthropic's systems within 30 days.

Personal accounts on the Free, Pro, or Max plan work differently. Since Anthropic's August 2025 consumer terms change, those conversations train future models unless the user turns training off in privacy settings, and conversations used for training are kept for up to five years. Anthropic's July 2026 privacy policy update added a detail worth knowing. Even with training turned off, a conversation that Anthropic's automated systems flag for safety review can still be used for model improvement, and flagged content is retained for up to two years. The opt-out is real, and it has a ceiling.

The practical starting point is which plan you're on. Many firms keep client work on a business plan, where the no-training commitment is contractual and the retention terms are written down. Either way, the Reg S-P vendor-oversight question from the last section still applies, because Anthropic processes whatever enters the conversation, training or not.

Claude for Work and Claude Enterprise also add administrative controls Anthropic markets toward regulated industries, including configurable data retention windows and activity logs an admin can review. None of that is a compliance certification by itself. It's infrastructure a firm's compliance program still has to evaluate, document, and monitor, the same as it would for any other vendor with access to anything client-related.

A solo advisor paying for Claude Pro out of pocket is on exactly the plan that trains by default. A larger RIA that negotiated a Claude for Work agreement for the whole team is not, though that same RIA still has to confirm procurement actually landed on a business plan and not a handful of individual Pro subscriptions advisors expensed on their own. The two setups can look identical day to day and carry different obligations underneath.

## What advisors use instead

Advisors who want the research and drafting benefit of a large language model without creating a new compliance exposure are moving toward a different structure. Instead of sending client files to an AI vendor, the AI reads the files where they already live, on the advisor's own computer, and only a narrow slice of nonclient information travels anywhere else.

Broadly, advisors evaluating AI tools are choosing between three structures. The first is a consumer AI tool used directly. The second is a hosted private AI platform, where a vendor still runs servers full of client data, just servers with the firm's name on the contract instead of the public tool, a structure that still leaves the same vendor-oversight and breach-notification questions in place, just with better paperwork behind them. The third keeps client files out of any new vendor's storage and has the AI read them locally instead, under the Claude plan the firm already holds.

**The common path.**

### Cloud AI tools

You paste a file, or type client details, into the chat.

The text travels to the vendor's servers.

The vendor's own policy decides what happens to it next.

From a regulator's view, it's now an undocumented service provider holding your client's data.

**What Briefly does instead.**

### Briefly inside Claude

You ask a question inside Claude.

Briefly reads the relevant file on your own computer.

Claude reads the file and Anthropic processes it, under your firm's own Claude plan.

Briefly's server sees your sign-in, a seat check, de-identified preference rules, and a short usage record for each tool call, never the file.

The left side is what happens with a consumer AI tool used directly. The right side is what happens when the same question runs through an AI knowledge base for financial advisors built to sit inside Claude instead of alongside it.

Briefly is built around the local path. It's a connector that runs inside Claude Desktop and fits a team that already works inside Claude day to day. Briefly also runs as a browser workspace for firms that would rather have Briefly handle the setup. An advisor using the connector points it at a folder of client documents, emails, and notes already stored on their computer. When they ask a question in Claude, Briefly reads the relevant files locally and writes the answer with the source cited. With the Briefly connector, client files never reach Briefly's servers. Only your sign-in, a seat check, de-identified preference rules, and a short usage record for each tool call do, and Claude reads the files under your firm's own Claude plan. Briefly is advisory-workflow software only, it reads files and never touches accounts, trading, or custody.

That's why the Reg S-P questions from earlier in this page narrow. Briefly never receives the client file, so there's nothing of your clients' on our servers to safeguard or disclose in a breach notice. Anthropic still processes what Claude reads, under the firm's own Claude plan, so that plan stays in your vendor file the way it already does today. What Briefly avoids adding is a second, unreviewed vendor holding client data.

This page covers the two most common paths. For a full comparison of what Claude can and can't see out of the box, and how advisors are giving it secure access to client files beyond Briefly, see Claude for financial advisors.

## Frequently asked questions

Q: Can financial advisors put client data into ChatGPT?

Typing a client's name, account number, or portfolio detail into ChatGPT sends that data to OpenAI's servers under a consumer agreement the firm never reviewed. The amended Reg S-P rule requires firms to oversee the service providers that handle customer information, and few firms have any oversight arrangement with OpenAI on file.

Q: Is ChatGPT compliant with SEC and FINRA rules for financial advisors?

ChatGPT itself isn't approved or rejected by the SEC or FINRA, and how an advisor uses it is what compliance programs look at. Pasting client information into the consumer chat window raises Reg S-P and recordkeeping questions firms are bringing to their compliance officers. General research or drafting with no client specifics raises far fewer of them.

Q: Does Regulation S-P apply to AI tools advisors use with client data?

The amended Reg S-P safeguards rule, in force for all RIAs since June 3, 2026, requires firms to oversee the third-party service providers that touch customer information, and an AI vendor receiving client data matches the kind of service provider the rule describes. The rule also calls for a written incident response program and a documented vendor review process.

Q: Can financial advisors use Claude for client work?

Yes, and the plan is what matters. Claude for Work, Enterprise, and API accounts fall under Anthropic's commercial terms, which state that Anthropic may not train models on customer content. Personal Free, Pro, and Max accounts train on conversations unless the user opts out, and safety-flagged chats can be used even after opting out. Many firms keep client work on a business plan for that reason.

Q: Does my firm need a written policy on AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude?

Many firms are writing one now. FINRA's 2026 oversight report says firms should assess and supervise their use of generative AI, and the SEC's 2026 exam priorities look at whether a firm's actual AI use matches what it discloses. Both reviews get easier to answer with a written policy naming which tools are approved, and what yours should say is a question for your compliance officer.

Q: Do advisors need to archive AI chat conversations under FINRA rules?

FINRA's books-and-records rules cover business correspondence broadly, and firms are asking their compliance officers whether an AI chat that drafts a client email or discusses an account functions as business correspondence under them. Most consumer AI chat tools were not built with archiving in mind.

Q: Is there an SEC-approved AI tool for financial advisors?

No, and no vendor can honestly claim that certification exists. The SEC fined two investment advisers, Delphia and Global Predictions, a combined $400,000 in 2024 for overstating their AI capabilities to clients. The lesson for advisors evaluating any AI tool, including Briefly, is to verify specific claims rather than trust a compliance label.

Q: What's the safest way for advisors to use AI with client information?

One structure keeps client files in the firm's own storage and has the AI read them there, under an agreement the firm has already reviewed. Briefly, an AI knowledge base for financial advisors, is built that way. Its connector runs inside Claude Desktop, client files never reach Briefly's servers, and only your sign-in, a seat check, de-identified preference rules, and a short usage record for each tool call do.

# Claude for Financial Advisors | Briefly
Source: https://www.brieflywealth.com/claude-for-financial-advisors

**Claude for Financial Advisors**

# What Claude can do for financial advisors, and what it still can't see.

By Connor Florczyk. Published July 23, 2026. Last verified August 5, 2026.

A plain look at what Claude handles out of the box, why your client files aren't part of that by default, and four ways to close the gap, ranked by where your data actually ends up.

A disclosure before this gets into it. Briefly is the local connector Briefly built, so this page isn't a neutral party on this topic. Everything below is written to hold up whether or not you ever install it, and the comparison further down scores Briefly's own product the same way it scores everyone else's.

## Why this question keeps coming up

Anthropic has been shipping finance-focused features on a fast clock, close to every ten weeks, and wealth firms keep getting pulled into the update cycle whether they asked for it or not. A sourced version of that timeline:

July 15, 2025. Anthropic launches Claude for Financial Services, with data connections to providers including S&P Global, Morningstar, and FactSet.

October 27, 2025. Anthropic adds a Claude for Excel plugin and new data connectors, including Moody's, aimed at teams that live in spreadsheets.

February 24, 2026. LPL Financial expands its partnership with Anthropic, bringing Claude to LPL's network of more than 30,000 affiliated advisors.

May 5, 2026. Anthropic ships ten ready-to-use agent templates for financial services plus full Microsoft 365 integration, adding still more data partners.

None of these releases close the client-file gap on their own. They put Claude in front of institutions and large broker-dealer networks like LPL's rather than in front of a solo advisor's desktop, which is exactly why the access methods further down this page exist.

## What Claude can already do for an advisor

Sign up for Claude and you get a capable general-purpose model with no advisor-specific features and no memory of your book of business. Inside that plain account, it's still useful for a lot of the writing and thinking work that fills an advisor's week.

Drafting client emails, letters, and meeting follow-ups from notes you type or paste in.

Summarizing a document you upload for that conversation, a fund prospectus or a financial plan.

Explaining a tax, estate, or planning concept in language you can hand to a client.

Checking the math on a projection or comparing two scenarios you describe.

Drafting notes ahead of a client meeting, if you paste the relevant background in yourself.

Brainstorming language for compliance-reviewed marketing copy or a client newsletter.

All of it works from what you type or paste into that one conversation. None of it involves Claude reaching out to your computer, your CRM, or your inbox unless you set that up separately.

## What Claude can't see, and why most comparisons skip it

Every new Claude conversation starts with nothing. No memory of a client from last week's chat, no access to the CRM record, no read on the plan you built in March. Claude only knows what you put in front of it, unless you've connected an outside source.

Most articles that compare Claude to other AI tools stop at capability, what it can write, summarize, or calculate, and skip the harder question of what it can reach. That's the decision an advisor actually has to make. Not whether Claude is smart enough, but how, and whether, to let it near client records at all.

## Claude connectors, in plain English

Claude can read from and act on other pieces of software through something called a connector, a small program that tells Claude how to talk to a particular system, whether that's Google Drive, a CRM, or a program running on your own computer. Most connectors, including the one Briefly runs, are built on the same open standard for how a model talks to outside tools and data. What matters is where the other end of the connector lives, on a vendor's server somewhere, or on your own machine.

## Claude, with and without a local connector

Here's what that looks like in practice. ChatGPT and Claude as they ship, next to Claude with the Briefly connector added.

Data access

Whatever you paste into the chat, plus files you upload for that one session, on ChatGPT.

Whatever you paste into the chat, plus any connected apps you've approved, like Drive or Gmail, on Claude.

With the Briefly connector, documents and notes in the folder you point Briefly at, read straight from your computer.

Remembers the client between sessions

Partly, on ChatGPT. Its memory can carry details between chats, but it lives in one person's account, with nothing your firm can review or cite.

No, not on its own, on Claude. You'd need to paste the background in again or keep a connector active.

Yes, with the Briefly connector. Briefly writes what it learns back to files on your computer, so the next conversation can pick up where the last one left off.

Where files live

On OpenAI's servers for that conversation, and potentially longer depending on your plan and settings, on ChatGPT.

With whichever vendor hosts the connector, Google or Microsoft in most cases, plus Anthropic's infrastructure while it's serving the connection, on Claude.

With the Briefly connector, files stay on your computer, in the folder you chose. Only your sign-in, a seat check, de-identified preference rules, and a short usage record for each tool call reach Briefly's server.

Compliance posture

You're relying on OpenAI's data policies and your own recordkeeping on ChatGPT. No features built for advisor compliance.

You're relying on Anthropic's data policies on Claude. Business plans are barred from training on your content by contract, and the recordkeeping question is still yours to answer.

With the Briefly connector, client files never reach Briefly's servers, so there's no client data on Briefly's end to govern, and Claude reads the files under the firm's own Claude plan. See the compliance page for the full accounting.

Setup effort

None on ChatGPT. Sign up and start typing.

Low on Claude. Sign up, connect an app or two if you want to.

With the Briefly connector, one download, pick a folder, sign in. A few minutes.

ChatGPT still wins in a few places worth naming honestly. It plugs into more outside tools today, its Code Interpreter is genuinely useful for one-off spreadsheet math, and most staff have already used it at home, so training time is close to zero. If those three things matter more to your firm than where client files end up, that's a reasonable call.

## How to give Claude access to client files securely

There are four common ways advisors connect Claude to something resembling client information, and they aren't equally safe. The list below is ranked from the least contained to the most.

### Pasting into the chat

You copy a client's situation, notes, or numbers directly into the conversation. It's the fastest way to get an answer, and also the method with the least oversight. That text becomes part of the conversation on Anthropic's servers, and depending on your plan, may be used to improve their models. Fine for a hypothetical or an already de-identified question. Risky for anything a client would recognize as their own.

### Claude's built-in connectors

Claude Desktop has a menu of connectors to apps you probably already use, Google Drive and Gmail among them. Anthropic's own infrastructure handles the connection, so your files stay wherever Google or Microsoft already stores them, but Claude, and by extension Anthropic, reads them during the conversation. No extra install, and one more company sitting in the data path.

### A vendor's own connector

Some financial software companies run their own connector into Claude the same way Anthropic does. In practice, this usually means the vendor holds a copy of your client data on their own servers so the connector has something to serve up when Claude asks for it. You're now trusting that company's security and retention practices on top of Anthropic's.

### A local connector that reads files from your machine

The connector runs on your own computer and reads files from a folder you choose. Claude asks it a question, the connector reads the answer off your machine's disk, and Anthropic processes what Claude reads under the firm's own Claude plan, the same model call every method on this list involves. The difference is storage, since this is the only one of the four where client files never end up copied onto a vendor's infrastructure, and it's the approach Briefly built its connector around. Client files never reach Briefly's servers. Only your sign-in, a seat check, de-identified preference rules, and a short usage record for each tool call do.

## What Claude handles well once it can see your files

The five examples below show up every week once Claude can read a client's files instead of relying on whatever an advisor remembered to type in. Each one assumes a local connector like Briefly's, which reads whatever sits in the folder you point it at and cites the specific file behind every number.

### Meeting prep from a folder of statements

Drop the last two or three custodian statements for a client into an intake folder and ask for a meeting brief. Claude reads each PDF, pulls the account values, contribution or withdrawal activity, and anything that changed since the last statement, then writes a short brief with every number cited back to the specific statement it came from. An advisor meeting a client Tuesday can drop Friday's statements in over the weekend and have a brief waiting Monday morning.

### Drafting a client email from a plan document

Point Claude at a financial plan already sitting in the folder and ask for a follow-up email explaining one recommendation in plain language, a Roth conversion amount, a new savings rate, a change to the glide path. Because it's reading the actual plan, the numbers in the draft match the document the client received.

### Summarizing a custodian PDF

A forty-page brokerage statement is not something anyone wants to read cover to cover before a call. Ask Claude to summarize holdings, cash flows, and anything that changed since the prior statement, and it comes back with a short summary citing the source PDF next to each figure.

### Checking concentration across accounts

A client holding the same stock in a taxable account, an IRA, and a 401(k) held away at a different custodian usually means opening three statements and adding the position up by hand. Claude can total that position across every statement on file and flag what share of the household's assets sit in one name, with the source statement cited for each account the number came from.

### Quarterly review notes

Ahead of a quarterly review, ask Claude to pull performance numbers, the notes from the last meeting, and any open follow-ups into one outline, with every figure in the outline traced back to the statement or note it came from.

The mechanism is the same in every example above. The connector hands Claude the actual file, and every answer points back to the line the number came from, instead of a fluent-sounding paragraph nobody can trace to anything.

## Getting started

Pick a Claude plan that matches how you'll use it. Anthropic's commercial terms bar training on customer content for Work, Enterprise, and API accounts, while personal plans train on conversations unless you opt out. Many firms keep client work on a business plan for that reason, and your compliance officer can weigh in on the right setup for yours.

Start with pasting or a built-in connector for occasional use.

If you want Claude reading your files regularly, decide between a vendor's own connector and a local connector based on where you're comfortable having that data sit.

If a local connector is what you want, Briefly is one option, an AI knowledge base for financial advisors that runs inside Claude and reads from a folder on your computer. See how it works, or look at sample deliverables to see what a brief looks like before you install anything.

## Frequently asked questions

Q: Can I use Claude for financial advisor work today?

Yes. Claude works like any general AI chat tool out of the box, drafting emails, summarizing documents you paste in, and explaining planning or tax concepts. It has no special financial advisor mode and no access to your client files unless you connect something yourself.

Q: What can Claude do without any extra setup?

Draft client communication, summarize a document you paste in, check math, explain a concept in plain language, and help write compliance-reviewed marketing copy. All of this works inside a plain Claude account. None of it involves Claude reading anything from your computer or your CRM on its own.

Q: Can Claude see my client files automatically?

No. A new Claude conversation starts with nothing about your clients unless you paste details in or connect a source yourself. Claude does not browse your computer, your CRM, or your email on its own.

Q: What is a Claude connector?

A Claude connector is a small program that lets Claude read and act on a firm's own systems and files, whether that's a calendar, a CRM, or a program running on your own computer. What matters is where the other end of the connector lives, a vendor's server or your own machine.

Q: Is it safe to paste client information directly into Claude?

It depends on your plan. On Claude for Work, Enterprise, and API accounts, Anthropic's commercial terms bar training on customer content. A personal account trains on conversations unless you opt out in settings, and safety-flagged chats can be used even then. There's also a recordkeeping question, since what you paste may count as business correspondence under your firm's own rules, which is worth confirming with your compliance officer.

Q: What's the difference between Claude's built-in connectors and a vendor's own connector?

Claude's built-in connectors, like Google Drive or Gmail, route through Anthropic's own infrastructure to reach an app you already use. A vendor's own connector works differently, and it often means the vendor has copied your data onto their servers so there's something for Claude to read.

Q: Does Claude remember a client from one conversation to the next?

Partly. Claude's memory is on by default now and carries context between conversations, so a client you discussed last week can come up again. That memory lives in one person's account though, where the firm can't review it, correct it, or cite it, and nobody else on the team inherits it. Briefly writes what gets learned about a client back to files your firm owns, so every advisor's next conversation starts from the same record, with citations.

Q: How is Briefly different from just using Claude on its own?

Briefly is an AI knowledge base for financial advisors that runs inside Claude as a local connector. It reads and writes files in a folder on your computer instead of a vendor's cloud, so Claude works from your actual client records and Briefly never holds a copy of them.

# The Jobs AI Won't Replace | Briefly
Source: https://www.brieflywealth.com/blog/jobs-ai-wont-replace
---

By Connor Florczyk. December 17, 2025. 2 min read.

# The Jobs AI Won't Replace

The professions people assume AI will replace first (financial advisors, lawyers, doctors, consultants) are actually the most protected. Not because the technology isn't advancing, but because these predictions misunderstand what the work actually is.

From a distance, these jobs look like information processing. Up close, they're trust, judgment, and accountability.

## Why Human Professionals Remain Essential

**Trust matters more than accuracy.** Only 28% of retail investors trust AI-generated investment recommendations. A majority of patients are uneasy receiving a diagnosis without a clinician present. The value of any plan depends on whether it can be carried out, and that requires human guidance through volatility and uncertainty.

**Professionals work with data AI never sees.** An estimated 80% of medical diagnoses come from patient history gathered through conversation and observation. Advisors recognize when stated risk tolerance doesn't match behavior. Attorneys sense tension before anything gets written down. Tone, hesitation, body language, context. None of this shows up in a spreadsheet.

**Responsibility can't be assigned to a model.** Advisors remain legally responsible for recommendations even when using AI analysis. Attorneys are accountable for any filing under their name. Physicians bear legal liability for clinical decisions. When things go wrong, people need someone to hold accountable. A system can't be sued.

## What Changes

AI will handle data-heavy, pattern-matching work that consumes professional time. It will surface insights faster and catch errors humans miss. The advisors, lawyers, and doctors who learn to work effectively with AI will dramatically outperform those who don't.

**But they'll still be needed for what they've always done: building trust, exercising judgment, taking responsibility, and helping people navigate decisions that matter.**

# Your Brain Doesn't Have Enough RAM | Briefly
Source: https://www.brieflywealth.com/blog/your-brain-doesnt-have-enough-ram
---

By Connor Florczyk. January 3, 2026. 3 min read.

# Your Brain Doesn't Have Enough RAM

You have 200 unread emails. Somewhere in there is a detail your client mentioned three weeks ago that you promised to follow up on. The meeting is in twenty minutes. This isn't a failure of effort. It's a failure of biology.

## The Core Problem

Dunbar's number limits us to roughly 150 meaningful relationships. The average financial advisor manages 100 households. A therapist sees 40 clients per week. A teacher has 150 students. Each relationship involves not just names and faces, but context, family dynamics, past conversations, unspoken concerns, and years of accumulated history.

Memory has hard limits. You can hold about four to seven things in your head at once. We forget roughly 70% of new information within a day unless we actively work to remember it. Task work gets completed. Relationship work accumulates indefinitely.

## Why Current Tools Fail

CRMs track the data. Email holds the conversations. Meeting notes capture the context. Portfolio systems show the numbers. But none of them talk to each other, and none of them know what you actually need to remember for the meeting in twenty minutes.

## The Real Constraint

The solution isn't to remember everything. It's to get the right information in front of you at the right time so your brain can focus on what it actually does well, reading people, understanding what someone values, and helping them navigate hard decisions.

No one can remember everything about 100 people across years of interactions. That's not a personal failure. It's just how humans work. The question is whether we're going to keep pretending otherwise, or build systems that let people focus on what makes them irreplaceable.

# The Great Wealth Transfer Trap | Briefly
Source: https://www.brieflywealth.com/blog/great-wealth-transfer-trap
---

By Connor Florczyk. November 5, 2025. 3 min read.

# The Great Wealth Transfer Trap

The promised $80 trillion wealth transfer isn't a windfall. It's an operational crisis. When a $10 million family divides across three heirs, the same assets require three times as many relationships to manage.

## The Core Problem

A typical advisor handles 100 households and $300M in AUM. If one-third of those families transfer wealth and fragment into 3-4 heir households, that book swells to 180 relationships. That's an 80% increase with zero additional revenue.

**The economics don't work:** Servicing 80% more households requires 70-90% more headcount. With compensation already consuming 50% of revenue, that math breaks the business model.

## The Real Bottleneck

Most wealth-tech tackles back-office efficiency: rebalancing, compliance, billing. But the true constraint is **front-office cognitive load:** preparing for meetings, following up, staying contextually relevant. Advisors spend 40% of their time on coordination that should take minutes.

**Automation can't scale trust.** Email templates reduce clicks, not mental friction. When data lives in silos, every meeting begins with manual reconstruction across CRMs, emails, and portfolio systems.

## The Market Reality

Global financial wealth hit $300 trillion in 2024, but organic growth among advisors has stalled.

One-third of households will change their primary advisor relationship within a decade.

Less than 25% of firms have integrated intelligent automation into client workflows.

Industry IP (understanding of relationships) remains unstructured and inaccessible.

Tools like Altruist, Addepar, and Orion have modernized execution. The white space is **relationship intelligence:** knowing who to call, what to say, when to reach out.

The next competitive edge goes to firms that can double relationship capacity without doubling staff. Those that preserve personalization while scaling from 100 to 200 clients per advisor.

**The future belongs to firms that scale context and trust.**
